europe.change: off the week's 1.1648 high, dollar bid pre-CPI

items.headline: Iran-US Gulf war escalates further, sending oil to fresh highs and driving a broad-based Asia risk-off
items.detail: Brent crude spiked as much as intraday to above $109 -- a fresh high in the current escalation -- after Iran reportedly struck ten vessels near the Strait of Hormuz in what Reuters called the largest declared wave of tit-for-tat shipping attacks since the war began, with additional blasts reported at Minab, Jask and Qeshm Island. The Strait has been effectively shut to normal commercial traffic since a US-Israeli strike campaign in late February, so today's escalation reads as an intensification of an already-live crisis rather than a fresh shock, and it landed directly on every regional equity benchmark: Nikkei -1.9%, Kospi -1.76%, Hang Seng -1%, ASX 200 -1.54%, CSI 300 -1.59%. The move also fed straight into rates, with JGB 10-year yields up 7.5bp to 2.985% and 20-year yields up 7bp to 3.82% as global bond markets sold off in sympathy with US Treasuries. Oil pared back to settle around $106.11 by mid-session as some of the risk premium unwound, but desks are treating $105-110 as the new working range for as long as the conflict continues, with Iran's negotiators showing no sign of a near-term de-escalation after July's ceasefire collapsed.
items.source: Al Jazeera, ABC News, Bloomberg, Reuters

items.headline: Nikkei slides 1.9% to 64,011 as yen firmness compounds an AI/semis-led selloff
items.detail: Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 1,259.61 points (-1.93%) to close at 64,011.34, having been down as much as nearly 3% intraday before paring losses, with Advantest the single biggest drag given its outsized index weighting and high valuation sensitivity to AI-capex sentiment, and Tokyo Electron close behind. The move compounds an ongoing yen story: USD/JPY has spent the week grinding down from above 155 to test seven-month lows below 153 on mounting BOJ rate-hike bets and reported US-Japan intervention, before steadying around 153.6 today as the dollar found a bid on hawkish Fed repricing. A stronger yen and pricier oil are a genuine double hit for Japan's exporters -- Toyota has flagged roughly Y50bn of lost operating income for every Y1 of yen appreciation -- while the chip-equipment complex is separately digesting a second straight day of profit-taking after this week's AI-infrastructure enthusiasm cooled. Friday's US CPI print, due after the Tokyo close, is being flagged by local desks as the next swing factor for both the yen and risk appetite into next week's BOJ and FOMC meetings.
items.source: News On Japan, Business Recorder, Bloomberg

items.headline: Kospi claws back most of a 3.3% opening plunge to close down 1.76% as chip stocks lead, but 'smart money' buys the dip
items.detail: South Korea's Kospi opened 3.29% lower at 6,802.50 before recovering through the session to close at 6,909.91, down 124.01 points (-1.76%), as overnight US tech weakness and the oil/Treasury-yield spike hit the index's heavily chip-concentrated composition. Samsung Electronics fell as much as 4.65% intraday before closing down 3.53% at 259,500 won, while SK Hynix dropped as much as 4.59% before settling down 2.21% at 1,812,000 won; foreign investors were heavy net sellers, offloading roughly 912bn won of Samsung and 1.07trn won of SK Hynix combined. Notably, Seoul Economic Daily reported that the country's top 1% of traders were net buyers into the weakness, using the pullback to add to positions in both chip bellwethers -- a domestic-retail-versus-foreign-institutional divergence worth flagging for anyone tracking Korean equity flows. Samsung and SK Hynix together still make up more than 40% of the Kospi, so the index's intraday round-trip is as much a story about a violent reversal in AI/memory sentiment as it is about the broader oil-driven risk-off.
items.source: Seoul Economic Daily, SBS News, Investing.com

items.headline: Hang Seng falls roughly 1% to ~24,691 as the Brent spike above $109 unsettles Hong Kong risk sentiment
items.detail: Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index dropped around 257 points to close near 24,691, extending Thursday's 1.43% decline, as crude's intraday push through $109 -- its highest level of the current Middle East escalation -- weighed on regional risk appetite and pressured long-duration China growth names that remain highly sensitive to global yields. The decline builds on a pattern seen all week of Hong Kong-listed China plays trading in close correlation with US rates and oil, in contrast to a comparatively more resilient mainland tape earlier in the week that had been supported by tech-sector strength (CSI Cloud Computing +4%, CSI AI +2.8%). With the index now down for a second straight session, desks are watching whether the mainland's tech-led outperformance can continue to offset the oil/rates drag, or whether today's move marks a broader convergence of onshore and offshore China sentiment to the downside.
items.source: Sunday Guardian, Business Recorder, Trading Economics

items.headline: CSI 300 and Shanghai Composite fall 1.6-1.8%, extending the property-versus-tech divergence in mainland China
items.detail: The CSI 300 closed down 1.59% at 4,476.18 and the Shanghai Composite fell 1.82% to 3,862.73, giving back the tech-led gains that had helped mainland indices outperform Hong Kong earlier in the week. The pullback tracks the same oil/yield-driven risk-off hitting the rest of the region rather than a China-specific catalyst, but it narrows the gap between onshore resilience and the broader regional selloff. Property names remain a separate, slower-burn drag: the Hang Seng Mainland Properties Index is down roughly 6% and onshore real-estate names around 3% since Beijing's mortgage-rule overhaul earlier this month, a structural overhang that continues to sit alongside the more headline-grabbing tech and AI-linked subindices. Desks sizing China beta should note that today's move compresses, but does not erase, the divergence between the country's AI/tech-driven equity enthusiasm and its still-weak property complex.

items.headline: ASX 200 drops 1.54% to 8,684 as RBA rate-hike odds for September 29 jump to 80%
items.detail: Australia's benchmark fell 1.54% to 8,684, adding to Thursday's roughly 1% decline, as the oil spike revived inflation concerns just over two weeks before the RBA's next decision. Money markets are now pricing an approximately 80% probability of a 25bp hike to 4.60% on September 29, up sharply from just 17% before the July CPI print in late August, with a former RBA official flagging the move could come alongside as much as a 10% correction in home prices. NAB continues to call for the hike in September, while ANZ, CBA and Westpac see it landing in November, but all four majors now agree at least one more hike is coming this year with trimmed-mean inflation stuck at 3.6%, above the RBA's 2-3% target band. The broad-based nature of the selloff -- echoing Thursday's pattern of red across every sector -- points to a genuine macro/rates repricing rather than an idiosyncratic story, leaving the index at fresh multi-week lows.

items.headline: JGB yields jump as all 52 BOJ watchers now see a September 18 hike to 1.25%, with 93% expecting a follow-up by January
items.detail: The benchmark 10-year JGB yield rose 7.5bp to 2.985% and the 20-year climbed 7bp to 3.82%, tracking a global bond selloff as oil concerns pushed US Treasury yields higher overnight. A Bloomberg survey found all 52 economists polled expect the BOJ to raise its policy rate at the end of the September 17-18 meeting, most likely by 25bp to 1.25% -- a level not seen in 31 years -- with 93% expecting a further move by January (a third of those seeing it as soon as December) and none predicting back-to-back hikes in October. Reuters-polled analysts see the path continuing to 1.5% by end-March and 1.75% in Q2 2027, a genuinely multi-year normalization trajectory that is running independently of, but now compounding, the oil-driven duration selloff hitting global rates markets this week. For rates desks, the read-through is that Japan's tightening cycle shows no sign of slowing even as broader risk sentiment sours, putting JGB yields on a converging path with a Fed that markets are now pricing to hike, not cut, at its own meeting next week.

items.headline: PBOC fixing keeps lagging the market by ~570 pips, a continued deliberate brake on yuan appreciation
items.detail: The PBOC set today's USD/CNY reference rate at 6.7743, modestly stronger for the yuan than Thursday's 6.7766 fix but still roughly 570 pips weaker than the market's 6.7174 estimate -- a gap traders continue to read as evidence the central bank wants to slow, not stop, the currency's appreciation. This is the second straight session the fixing has landed meaningfully on the strong-dollar side of market expectations, extending the pattern flagged in Thursday's session, even as the offshore CNH spot rate has continued to grind toward its strongest levels since February 2023. The yuan's strength is being helped by broad dollar softness and reduced capital-outflow pressure, but China is still leaning on the export channel for growth (trade surplus running near $806bn on a trailing basis), so a currency appreciating too quickly would erode competitiveness at an awkward moment. FX and macro desks should keep watching the fixing-versus-estimate gap as the cleanest real-time signal of the PBOC's tolerance band being tested.

items.headline: Indian rupee grinds to ~95.79, record-low territory, despite RBI's near-daily intervention
items.detail: USD/INR weakened 27 paise to around 95.79 in early trade, extending a multi-week slide as Brent's push above $108 outweighs the Reserve Bank of India's persistent defense of the currency. The RBI is estimated to have sold at least $8bn last week alone, with state banks reportedly offering dollars whenever the rupee weakens rather than defending a hard line -- a pattern consistent with smoothing a managed depreciation rather than fighting the underlying trend. India remains one of Asia's most oil-import-dependent large economies, so today's fresh leg higher in crude is a direct terms-of-trade hit, compounded by continued foreign portfolio outflows. With Brent now trading in a $105-110 range for as long as the Gulf conflict continues, desks running EM Asia FX risk see little near-term relief for the rupee absent either a ceasefire or a materially larger RBI intervention push.

items.headline: AUD/USD falls 0.9% to 0.7154 as hawkish RBA repricing collides with broad risk-off
items.detail: The Australian dollar dropped to 0.7154, a clean, tradable single-asset move that sits at the intersection of two forces working in the same direction: a domestic rates story (RBA hike odds for September 29 now at 80%, versus 17% a month ago) that would normally support the currency, and a broader oil-driven risk-off that is instead dominating price action given AUD's status as a high-beta risk proxy. The net effect illustrates a common pattern in this kind of cross-asset shock -- a hawkish domestic repricing gets overwhelmed by a global growth/inflation scare -- and leaves the currency near its softest levels of the week even as rate-differential support should, in isolation, be building. FX desks are watching whether the RBA decision itself, when it lands on September 29, can finally decouple AUD from the oil/risk-sentiment complex that has dominated its price action this week.

items.headline: USD/KRW grinds toward ~1,386, near cycle highs, as chip-sector foreign outflows add to won pressure
items.detail: The won continues to trade on the back foot near 1,386 per dollar, close to its recent range highs, as today's heavy foreign net selling in Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix (a combined roughly 2 trillion won) adds a portfolio-outflow channel on top of the broader dollar-firming, risk-off backdrop. With Samsung and SK Hynix together representing over 40% of the Kospi's market cap, swings in foreign positioning in those two names have an outsized, near-mechanical effect on won demand relative to most other Asian currencies. This remains a clean, quantifiable FX-flow story for anyone running Korea or broader Asia-tech currency exposure, particularly given how correlated the won has become with global AI/semiconductor sentiment this year.

items.headline: Asia dollar-bond primary market stays busy, led by a $3.5bn MUFG deal, as issuers rush to lock in funding
items.detail: Borrowers from around the Asia-Pacific region continued to crowd into the dollar bond market this week, with more than ten issuers pricing transactions including Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group's $3.5bn offering -- Japan's largest bank tapping the market in one of the busiest sessions of the year regionally, part of a global session that raised more than $70bn, the most since June. The rush reflects issuers seeking to lock in funding ahead of any further rate increases, with Asia credit spreads sitting near the tight end of their historical range after a year of steady compression -- healthy fundamentals and greater currency diversification in issuance are cited as support, though the tight starting point means further spread compression looks limited from here. For L/S credit and Asia fixed-income allocators, the setup argues that incremental returns are more likely to come from carry than from further tightening, a dynamic that hasn't yet been meaningfully disrupted by this week's equity-level volatility.

items.headline: Korean defense and industrial names land large overseas contracts amid the geopolitical backdrop
items.detail: Samsung E&A won a $3.5bn EPC contract to build a fertilizer production facility in Saudi Arabia, while Hanwha Aerospace signed a 641.1bn won (roughly $460mn) deal to export Chunmoo multiple rocket launchers to Croatia's Ministry of Defense. Neither deal is a market-moving catalyst on its own, but both fit a pattern this year of Korean industrial and defense names picking up large overseas orders even as the broader Kospi wobbles on chip-sector volatility, echoing the way defense contractors have outperformed elsewhere in the region on contractually locked-in backlogs that are largely insulated from day-to-day macro swings. It's a useful reminder for single-name and sector-rotation desks that Korea's equity story this year isn't solely a semiconductor/AI narrative -- industrial EPC and defense-export franchises are quietly compounding their own order books alongside it.

items.headline: Gold holds a choppy range near $4,365-4,410 as safe-haven demand tussles with a firmer dollar
items.detail: Spot gold continues to trade in a wide band roughly between $4,365 and $4,410/oz, essentially the same range it has occupied since Wednesday, as the ongoing Gulf escalation's safe-haven bid is offset by a dollar that firmed on Thursday's hot PPI print and rising Fed-hike odds for next week's FOMC. Global gold ETFs pulled in $17.9bn in August alone -- the second-largest monthly intake on record -- underscoring that institutional demand for the hedge remains structurally strong even with gold roughly 22% below its January 2026 record above $5,589. With oil now carrying much of the day's fresh geopolitical risk premium, gold's relatively muted reaction suggests a large portion of the escalation is already priced in, though a further widening of the conflict would likely reignite the bid more aggressively.
items.source: World Gold Council, Kobeissi Letter, market data

items.headline: Copper eases to $6.46/lb but remains up roughly 41% year-on-year on structural AI/data-center demand
items.detail: Copper slipped a further 0.07% to $6.46/lb, extending a modest pullback from its highs but still up about 41% over the past year, a run driven primarily by AI/data-center-linked demand growth and tight concentrate supply rather than the broader macro cycle. Today's softness looks more like risk-off spillover from the equity selloff than any change to the underlying structural demand story, and copper remains one of the year's standout commodity performers even after giving back some ground over the past month.

items.headline: Hot US core CPI sends Fed hike odds for next week to ~85%, dollar bid and Treasury yields toward 5% -- a mid-afternoon regime shift for European desks
items.detail: August US CPI printed a headline 0.4% m/m (3.4% y/y) that was in line with consensus, but core CPI came in at 0.3% m/m -- a tenth above the 0.2% forecast, with 12-month core steady at 2.4% -- and that core beat was enough to push CME-tracked odds of a 25bp Fed hike at next Wednesday's FOMC to roughly 85-86%, up from just 48% a month ago and 71% ahead of Thursday's hot PPI. The release landed at 14:30 CEST, squarely inside the European afternoon session, and the reaction was immediate and cross-asset: the 10-year Treasury yield pushed to within a whisker of the psychologically important 5% level (4.95-4.96%, the highest since 2023), the dollar firmed against every major, and European government bonds sold off in sympathy on top of their own ECB-driven repricing. Kobeissi Letter flagged the m/m core print as the largest increase since May and noted markets began 2026 pricing a third Fed cut for September, a full reversal now underway as inflation "roars on." For European rates and FX desks the read-through is that the transatlantic hiking cycle is now a two-central-bank story rather than an ECB-only one, tightening the correlation between Bund/Gilt and Treasury yields into next week's back-to-back FOMC and BOJ decisions.
items.source: Bloomberg, CNBC, Kobeissi Letter, CME FedWatch (via 24/7 Wall St.)

items.headline: Gulf war widens to a new Lebanon front and a Houthi push into the Red Sea; Brent hits a fresh $109.97 high before easing on a Monday Oman-meeting report
items.detail: The Middle East conflict that has dominated Asia and European trading all week escalated further overnight and into Friday: Israeli strikes on southern Lebanon killed at least 11 people as Israel-Hezbollah clashes intensified, while Houthi forces advanced along Yemen's coast to the Hanish Islands, opening a de facto new front near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait alongside the existing US-Iran fighting around Hormuz. Brent crude spiked to $109.97 a barrel intraday -- a fresh high for the current escalation, last seen in early May -- before paring back toward $106 on reports that Gulf states and Iran will meet in Oman on Monday to discuss restoring shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the first concrete diplomatic signal in weeks. The widening of hostilities beyond the original Hormuz theatre into Lebanon and the southern Red Sea is the key escalation risk European desks are now pricing: it raises the odds that the conflict disrupts a second major shipping corridor simultaneously, which would be a materially larger supply shock than the Hormuz blockade alone. European natural gas, defense equities and the euro all took direction from this story today, and the Oman meeting on Monday is now the single most-watched near-term catalyst for European risk assets.
items.source: CNBC, Confluence Investment Management, Bloomberg Oil Market news

items.headline: Bund yield climbs to 3.51%, a 17-year high, as ECB's hawkish Thursday hike keeps repricing through Friday's session
items.detail: Germany's 10-year Bund yield rose a further 2bp to 3.51% -- its highest level since August 2009 -- extending Thursday's move after the ECB raised its deposit rate 25bp to 2.50% (main refinancing rate to 2.65%) and explicitly flagged upside inflation risk from the energy shock, with Lagarde warning the energy shock "could intensify further" and its pass-through to core prices and wages could be stronger than currently modeled. The ECB's own projections now see core inflation at 2.5-2.6% through 2027 and headline staying above target into H1 2027, and interest-rate futures are pricing roughly a third hike by December even though Lagarde pointedly declined to pre-commit to a path. The follow-through today shows the market treating Thursday's decision as the start of a cycle rather than a one-off: Bund yields are still climbing a full session later, a pattern consistent with a genuine repricing of the ECB's reaction function rather than a one-day knee-jerk move. For European rates desks, the setup mirrors the JGB story flagged in Asia earlier this week -- a major DM central bank hiking into a supply-side inflation shock -- and argues for continued curve-flattening pressure as front-end expectations catch up to the hawkish guidance.
items.source: ING Think, FXStreet, Morningstar, ECB press conference transcript
items.time: European session, extending Thursday's ECB decision

items.headline: Gilts ease off a 19-year high near 5.38% but remain close to it as BOE hike bets build alongside the ECB and Fed
items.detail: UK 10-year gilt yields eased slightly toward 5.35% on Friday after touching 5.378% on Thursday -- the highest level since 2007 -- as energy prices retreated modestly from their overnight spike, while 30-year gilts sit near 5.95% after rising 8bp on Thursday. The move continues a multi-week gilt selloff driven by the same combination hitting Bunds and Treasuries: energy-driven inflation risk from the Gulf conflict compounding an already-hawkish global rates backdrop, with UK natural gas prices at their highest since late 2022. The UK's fiscal and inflation position leaves gilts structurally more exposed to an energy shock than Bunds given Britain's higher import dependence and the lingering premium priced into long-dated UK debt since the 2022 mini-budget episode, so the 30-year's persistence near cycle highs is arguably the more telling signal than the modest pullback at the 10-year point. Rates desks running UK duration risk should note the gilt curve has now round-tripped through a full year of BOE-hike repricing in a matter of weeks, a pace that leaves limited room for error if Monday's Oman talks produce any de-escalation.
items.source: Trading Economics, Bank of England data

items.headline: European equities bounce 0.5-0.9% into the weekend but are still headed for their worst week in about two months
items.detail: The Euro Stoxx 50 rose 0.9% to 6,327, the DAX and CAC 40 both added roughly 0.8%, and the FTSE 100 gained just over 0.5% to close at 14,404 -- continental markets outperforming London by roughly half a point, consistent with sterling assets facing more BOE-hike-related uncertainty than the euro bloc. The pan-European STOXX 600 was up 0.4% at 638.63 by mid-morning (0837 GMT). Despite the Friday bounce, the index closed at a two-month low on Thursday after the ECB's hike and hawkish guidance, and the week overall remains the sharpest weekly decline in about two months as elevated bond yields and rate-hike fears offset any relief from oil pulling back off its highs. The divergence between a green tape today and a red week overall is the clearest single-asset-class signal in Europe right now: desks are treating today's gain as short-covering into the weekend ahead of Monday's Oman talks rather than a genuine turn, given the Bund and gilt yield backdrop hasn't actually improved.
items.source: Business Recorder, Reuters (via Yahoo Finance), WTVB

items.headline: FTSE MIB and IBEX 35 lag the continental bounce, both modestly lower as Italian and Spanish single names diverge
items.detail: Spain's IBEX 35 fell 0.18% to 19,659.8, dragged by ACS (-4.44%), ArcelorMittal (-2.59%) and Puig (-2.18%), while gains in Solaria Energia (+1.85%) only partly offset the losses. Italy's FTSE MIB closed Thursday down 0.13% at 51,807, with Moncler (-2.93%), Avio (-2.74%) and Buzzi Unicem (-2.71%) the biggest drags against gains in Lottomatica (+4.68%) and Leonardo (+3.22%). Both indices are underperforming the DAX/CAC/Euro Stoxx 50 bounce by a full percentage point or more, a periphery-versus-core divergence that's worth flagging for anyone running dispersion or relative-value equity books in Europe, though neither move is large enough on its own to point to a distinct Italy or Spain-specific catalyst beyond idiosyncratic single-name weakness (ArcelorMittal on steel/commodity read-through, Moncler and Puig on the same luxury-demand concerns hitting LVMH and Hermes).

items.headline: European banks outperform again -- Santander +1.3%, BBVA +1% -- as higher-for-longer rates keep supporting net interest margins
items.detail: Spanish banks led the sector higher, with Santander up 1.3% and BBVA up 1% as the same ECB/Fed/BOE hawkish repricing that is hurting duration-sensitive names is a direct tailwind for bank net interest margins, extending a pattern that has held for European financials through most of this tightening episode. Banking stocks were flagged as among the STOXX 600's top performers today even as the broader tape digests a week of yield-curve pain, underscoring that the sector-rotation dynamic within Europe (banks/energy up, duration-sensitive luxury/tech down) mirrors the AI-versus-value rotation seen in Asia and the US this week. For single-name and sector-rotation desks, European banks remain one of the cleanest expressions of the "higher rates for longer" trade in the region, with Southern European banks (Santander, BBVA, Italian names) showing the most torque given their historically higher loan-to-deposit sensitivity to policy rates.

items.headline: LVMH and Hermes claw back modest gains off multi-year lows, but both remain down 34-37% YTD on the luxury demand slowdown
items.detail: LVMH traded around EUR409.20 in early trading, up roughly 0.7% from Thursday's multi-year-low close near EUR405.50, while Hermes rose about 0.6% to roughly EUR1,417 after closing near its 52-week low of EUR1,404 on Thursday. Both stocks remain down sharply for the year -- LVMH -37% YTD, Hermes -34% YTD -- despite double-digit revenue growth in recent results, as Q3 industry data points to a roughly 3-percentage-point slowdown in global luxury demand versus Q2, concentrated in the US, Japan and South Korea. This is a genuine sector-wide single-asset-class move with clear read-through: Moncler (-2.93% Thursday) and Puig (-2.18% today) are showing the same pattern, and the group's persistent underperformance despite still-strong reported growth numbers suggests the market is pricing a forward demand deceleration that hasn't yet shown up in the hard data -- a valuation-versus-fundamentals gap that L/S equity and consumer-sector desks should keep watching closely into the next reporting cycle.
items.source: ad-hoc-news.de, Global Banking and Finance, Morningstar

items.headline: Dutch TTF gas eases 1.6-2.5% after a five-session rally, still up 12% on the week as Hormuz/Red Sea disruption keeps a floor under prices
items.detail: The Dutch front-month TTF contract fell around 2.5% to roughly EUR77.60/MWh (a separate read put EU gas at EUR80.75/MWh, -1.57% on the day), pulling back from Thursday's EUR79.64 peak but still up 12.1% for the week as the Hormuz blockade and now the Red Sea/Houthi escalation continue to disrupt an estimated 20% of global LNG flows, primarily Qatari cargoes. The pullback tracks the same modest oil retracement (Brent off its $109.97 high) rather than any resolution of the underlying supply risk, and desks should treat today's dip as consistent with the broader "priced for de-escalation talks, not yet delivered" tone across European risk assets ahead of Monday's Oman meeting. Gas is arguably the cleanest read on how seriously the market takes the Gulf conflict's supply-chain risk to Europe specifically, given the continent's direct LNG dependence, and the fact it's still up double-digits on the week despite today's pullback signals the underlying risk premium hasn't gone anywhere.

items.headline: Rheinmetall falls a further ~2.8% to EUR988, extending the German defense sector's slide after Berlin's F126 naval program cancellation
items.detail: Rheinmetall shares dropped to around EUR988.35 from Thursday's EUR1,016.40 close, a roughly 2.8% decline that adds to the stock's ~35% drawdown from its 52-week high of EUR2,008, as the sector continues to digest Berlin's cancellation of the F126 frigate program -- a contract that could have been worth more than EUR12 billion with Rheinmetall as likely lead contractor. The broader German/European defense complex (Hensoldt, Renk, Saab, Leonardo, BAE Systems) has been under similar pressure in recent sessions as investors increasingly question how much of Europe's announced rearmament spending will actually convert into contractor backlogs versus remaining at the announcement stage. This is a useful counter-narrative to the "European defense as structural growth story" thesis that dominated 2025 positioning -- procurement-program risk is proving to be a real and recurring drag even with defense budgets nominally rising across the continent, and single-name/sector desks should treat government program cancellations, not just top-line budget headlines, as the key swing factor for the group going forward.

items.headline: EUR/USD softens toward 1.1615, GBP/USD falls in sympathy, EUR/GBP capped near 0.8600 ahead of the US CPI print
items.detail: EUR/USD traded around 1.1615, down from the week's 1.16475 high and toward Friday's 1.1592 low, as fresh dollar demand built ahead of the US CPI release; GBP/USD moved in the same direction as EUR/USD despite the ECB decision having no direct read-through to sterling, reflecting the pair's persistently high correlation with the euro. EUR/GBP held a neutral bias with 0.8600 capping the upside, a level FXStreet flagged as the key near-term resistance. The moves are modest, single-asset-class FX flows rather than anything cross-asset-defining on their own, but they set up the more consequential post-CPI dollar strength (see the Fed-odds item above) that hit European currencies harder into the afternoon.

items.headline: EM/periphery FX mixed: Turkish lira grinds to a fresh record low near 48.08, Polish zloty little changed, South African rand modestly firmer
items.detail: USD/TRY traded at 48.0803, up marginally from Thursday's 48.0338 close and continuing to press record-low territory for the lira (48.5 touched earlier this month) despite ongoing Central Bank of Turkey intervention to slow the slide; the lira is down 17.4% over the past 12 months. USD/PLN was little changed at 3.7266 versus 3.7220, while USD/ZAR eased about 0.3% to 16.15 from 16.1958, continuing the rand's slow structural firming trend (-7.8% over the past year) even as broader EM sentiment takes its cue from the Gulf conflict and the dollar's CPI-driven bid. None of these moves individually clears the bar for a standalone tradable catalyst today, but they're worth tracking as context: Turkey's currency defense is becoming a slower and more grinding story rather than a sharp devaluation event, which is itself notable for EM desks pricing intervention capacity.

items.headline: European corporate-action flow stays active: TotalEnergies-Shell renewables deal, Airbus/Leonardo/Thales JV filing, Accel-KKR/Eleco, MPS-Generali/BPM regulatory steps
items.detail: TotalEnergies completed its acquisition of Shell's entire European onshore renewables business, including a 1.2GW solar/wind portfolio (500MW operational, 3.5GW in development), with TotalEnergies simultaneously selling a 50% stake in the combined portfolio to KKR -- consistent with the sector's pattern of oil majors recycling renewables capital rather than retreating from the space entirely, even amid a windfall year for fossil-fuel trading profits. Separately, per MLex's antitrust round-up, Airbus, Leonardo and Thales are preparing to file their long-discussed space/defense joint venture to EU competition authorities, Accel-KKR is acquiring UK software company Eleco, MPS has begun the regulatory process around its stakes in Generali and BPM, and Heineken's acquisition of Stëlz is under Dutch regulatory review. None of these individually move markets, but the breadth of live European corporate-action flow -- spanning energy, aerospace/defense consolidation, financial-sector stakes and UK software M&A -- is itself a useful cross-check that deal activity hasn't frozen despite the volatile macro backdrop.
items.source: ESG Today, OilPrice.com, MLex Antitrust Press Round-Up

items.headline: European credit stays structurally tight even as rates rise, though pockets of IT services/software paper have widened over 200bp this year
items.detail: Despite the sharp rise in benchmark government yields across Germany, the UK and now the US, European credit spreads remain near the tight end of their historical range, with competition among lenders and thin net issuance reaffirming a borrower's-market dynamic in both public and private credit channels. The exception is idiosyncratic: B-rated European secondary loan spreads have widened roughly 65bp versus year-end 2025, and credits within IT services and software have widened by more than 200bp in some instances, though the broader move has proved shallow and short-lived rather than a systemic repricing. For L/S credit and multi-strategy desks, the setup argues that the base-rate move (Bund/gilt yields at multi-year highs) is a bigger risk to total-return credit portfolios right now than spread widening, since spreads themselves have barely budged outside a handful of stressed sub-sectors -- a dynamic that closely mirrors the Asia dollar-credit story flagged in Wednesday's Asia panel.

items.headline: CTAs continue rebuilding long equity exposure into September as realized volatility declines, a background tailwind for the risk-asset bounce
items.detail: Systematic trend-following strategies (CTAs) have been steadily rebuilding exposure from their July lows through late August, with the largest increases concentrated in US large- and small-cap futures as realized volatility ground lower over the summer. That positioning backdrop is relevant to today's European bounce: a systematic community that had been under-positioned into the recent Gulf-war/rates volatility provides a mechanical source of dip-buying flow on quieter sessions like today, even as the fundamental backdrop (yields, oil, geopolitics) remains unresolved. Multi-manager and macro-fund desks tracking CTA/trend positioning should note this is a slow-moving, backward-looking signal -- a renewed vol spike from either the Oman talks disappointing or a hot US CPI follow-through into next week could just as quickly reverse the rebuild.
